title: Attack and defend: a phishing campaign
blurb: Take apart a phishing email, find the forged headers, and layer email, DNS and identity defenses against it.
purpose: Phishing is the most common first step of a real attack. In this lab you learn the signs of a phishing message and see which Cisco controls stop it at each stage, from the mail gateway to DNS to the endpoint.
scenario: Several employees received an email that looks like it's from IT: "Your mailbox is full, sign in to keep your messages." One user clicked. Work out how the message got through, and add layers so the next campaign fails.
topology: Attacker ── Internet ── Secure Email Gateway ── mailbox ── user ── Umbrella DNS
objectives: Recognize the warning signs in a phishing message
Read the authentication results in the headers

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.learn: Phishing relies on **urgency**, **authority** and **look-alike** names. Teach users to check the real sender and the real link target, not the display name and link text.
steps.task: Pick every warning sign in this message.
steps.question:
From: "IT Service Desk" <helpdesk@scor-lab-support.com>
Subject: URGENT: Mailbox 98% full, action required within 2 hours
Link text: https://mail.scor.lab/quota  (actual target: https://scor-lab-support.com/owa/login.php)

options.text: The sender's domain is a look-alike, not scor.lab.
The link text and the real link target don't match.

options.why: Real IT messages mention mailboxes too. That alone isn't suspicious.

steps.title: Read the headers
steps.learn: Receiving servers record the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results in the **Authentication-Results** header. A look-alike domain can pass all three for itself. What protects you is that it isn't **your** domain.
steps.task: The header says: `spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=scor-lab-support.com; dkim=pass header.d=scor-lab-support.com; dmarc=pass header.from=scor-lab-support.com`. Answer the questions.

fields.label: Did SPF, DKIM and DMARC stop this message?
options: No, it passed for the attacker's own domain
fields.answer: No, it passed for the attacker's own domain

fields.label: What would catch a look-alike domain?
options: Newly registered and look-alike domain detection with sender reputation
fields.answer: Newly registered and look-alike domain detection with sender reputation

steps.title: Layer the defenses
steps.learn: No single control stops all phishing, so stack them. One control works before delivery, one at the click, and one if credentials are stolen anyway.
steps.task: Pick the control that fits each layer.

fields.label: Before delivery
options: Secure Email: sender reputation, URL rewriting and Forged Email Detection
Umbrella blocking the phishing domain at DNS
fields.answer: Secure Email: sender reputation, URL rewriting and Forged Email Detection

fields.label: When the user clicks
options: Secure Email: sender reputation, URL rewriting and Forged Email Detection
Umbrella blocking the phishing domain at DNS
fields.answer: Umbrella blocking the phishing domain at DNS

fields.label: If the password is stolen anyway
options: Secure Email: sender reputation, URL rewriting and Forged Email Detection
Umbrella blocking the phishing domain at DNS

steps.title: Respond
steps.task: One user entered their password. Put the response steps in order.
steps.question: Order from first to last.
items: Reset the user's password and revoke their active sessions
Block the phishing domain in Umbrella and on the email gateway
Search all mailboxes for the message and remove it
Review the account's sign-in logs and mailbox rules for attacker activity
Send a short awareness note to staff with the real indicators

summary: Look-alike domains, urgency and mismatched links as warning signs, authentication results that pass for the attacker's own domain, layered email, DNS and MFA controls, and the response order after a click.
